Let’s get an annulment.” mahina niyang sabi habang binabawi ang kamay niya. Unti-unting lumabo ang paningin niya dahil sa kirot. Kumunot ang noo nito. Halatang hindi inaasahan ang sasabihin niya. Nagkaroon ng sandaling katahimikan. Pagkatapos, tinawag nito ang waiter at humingi ng malinis na bowl. Kumuha siya ng piraso ng isda at maingat na tinanggal ang mga tinik gamit ang chopsticks. Habang ginagawa iyon, mahina at kalmadong nagsalita, “Kate, I know you’re still angry. Pero ang pagbanggit ng annulment, hindi ‘yan rational. Pag naghiwalay tayo, ano ang gagawin mo? How will you live alone?” Biglang bumilis ang paghinga ni Kate. Sa loob ng limang taon, sa mata ng lahat, isa lang siyang anino ni Vincent. Isang taong umaasa. At kung mawala si Vincent sa buhay niya, wala na siya. Isang babaeng walang silbi, walang pupuntahan, hindi kayang mabuhay mag-isa. Ganun din ang tingin nito sa kanya. “Kaya ko!” unang beses nlsiyang naging matapang sa harap nito. Unang beses niyang ipinaglaban ang sarili niya, kahit nanginginig ang boses. Ngunit ngumiti lang si Vincent. Para sa kanya, isa lang itong tampo. Isang sumpong ng emosyon. Inilapag niya ang isdang wala nang tinik sa harap ni Kate. “Kumain ka muna. You’re allowed to be angry a little longer, but after we eat, bawal na ang tampo.” “Hindi ako galit. I’m serious. Gusto ko talagang makipag-hiwalay!” giit niya pa. Paano ba niya sasabihin para maintindihan ni Vincent na hindi ito simpleng galit lang? “Kate.” ibinaba niya ang chopsticks. “Enough. I cancelled two meetings and one business appointment today just to be with you. Tomorrow and the next day, I might not even have time. Let me be clear…Mitch is our good friend. She’s one of us, one of my sisters. The way I treat her is no different from how I treat Norman and the others. She likes you too, she wants to be friends with you. With this attitude of yours, how can I even bring her to you?” “Then don’t bring her at all.” diretso niyang sagot. Hindi nlsiya kailanman naniwala na gusto talaga ni Mitch na maging kaibigan siya. “Kate!” may bahid na ng inis ang boses ni Vincent. Alam na alam niya, tuwing si Mitch ang usapan, nawawala ang pasensya ni Vincent. “Kumain ka na. After this, we’ll go to the mall, buy what you like, then dinner at my parents’ place. Kailan ka huling umuwi para bisitahin ang parents mo?” tuloy-tuloy niyang nilalagyan ng pagkain ang mangkok niya. Ayaw niyang pabayaan ang sarili niya. Kinuha niya ang kutsara at kumain. Hindi niya dapat parusahan ang sarili niya dahil lang sa sama ng loob. Hindi dapat idamay ang tiyan sa digmaan ng damdamin. Kailangan niyang maging malusog para sa sarili niya. “That’s better.” bumalik ang lambing sa boses ni Vincent. “Yung salitang ‘annulement’—huwag mo nang banggitin ulit. Ever.” Sandaling huminto si Kate, saka muling yumuko at kumain. Pagkatapos kumain, ayaw na sana niyang mag-mall. Pagod na siya—emosyonal at pisikal. Pero ipinilit ni Vincent. Diretso silang pumunta sa mall. Sa limang taon ng kanilang kasal, bilang lang sa daliri ang mga pagkakataong sinamahan siya ni Vincent sa mall. Mas tama sigurong sabihin bihira silang magpakita sa publiko bilang mag-asawa. Maliwanag ang ilaw ng mall kahit umaga. Nakasisilaw. Hindi siya sanay. Hawak ang bag, tahimik siyang naglakad sa likod ni Vincent at nananatili sa anino nito. Sa first floor—mga luxury bags, mamahaling relo, at alahas. “What do you want to buy?” tanong niya, humarap sa kanya. Wala siyang gustong bilhin. Gusto lang niyang umuwi. Pero bago pa siya makapagsalita, may tumawag mula sa malayo…“President Vincent!” “One of our new partners. I’ll say hi.” paalala niya. “You look around first. I’ll find you later.” Hindi niya kilala ang mga kausap ni Vincent. Habang nakikipagkamay ito sa isang lalaki sa di-kalayuan, nanatili siyang nakatayo. Sa gitna ng lahat ng karangyaan, wala siyang gustong paglaanan. “Miss, it’s your turn.” paalala ng saleslady. Doon niya napansin na nakapila pala siya sa isang luxury store. “Ah… no, thank you.” mabilis niyang sabi at agad umalis. Wala siyang direksyon habang naglalakad sa mall. Hanggang sa isang branded watch counter na may nakita siyang pamilyar na pigura. Si Mitch. Napatingin siya sa brand ng relo. May biglang lumubog sa dibdib niya. Hindi niya napigilan ang sarili at lumapit siya. Kasama ni Mitch si Norman. Habang papalapit siya, mas naging malinaw ang usapan nila. “If you like it, just buy it.” sabi ni Norman. “Isn’t it too much? This is really expensive. Even if Vincent gave me his supplementary card and told me to swipe freely, nakakahiya pa rin na ganito kamahal.” sagot ni Mitch. Huminto ang mga paa ni Kate. Parang biglang bumigat ang buong katawan niya. Supplementary card…Ang credit card niya. “If he gave it to you, it means he wants you to use it. Kailan ba naging plastic si Vincent? We’ve been friends for years—you know him. If he gives, he gives sincerely.” tuloy ni Norman. “That’s true…” sabi ni Mitch habang iniikot ang pulso niya, tinitingnan ang relo sa iba’t ibang anggulo. Nakita rin iyon ni Kate. “Maganda ba, Norman? I really, really love this watch. College pa lang ako gusto ko na ito. Vincent even promised he’d buy it for me after graduation. Then…” Then? Napangiti si Kate—mapait, puno ng panunuya sa sarili. Then, taon-taon, tuwing birthday niya at tuwing anniversary nila, iyon ang regalong ibinibigay sa kanya ni Vincent. Parehong relo. Parehong modelo. Akala niya noon, kahit wala itong puso, kahit malamig, kahit papaano, naaalala nito ang birthday niya. Ang anniversary nila. Akala niya, kahit walang effort, at least mahal ang regalo. Ngayon, saka lang niya naintindihan hindi pala walang puso si Vincent. Hindi pala siya walang effort. Sobrang may puso siya. Sobrang may effort. Pero ang laman ng pusong iyon ay hindi siya. “So I guess he’s fulfilling his promise now. You can buy anything you want. As long as you like it, he can afford it.” pang-uudyok ni Norman. “Then… I’ll swipe?” halatang tinamaan si Mitch. Sa di-kalayuan, tapos na si Vincent makipag-usap sa ka-partner niya. Nalaman din nitong kasama niya ang asawa niya kaya iminungkahi nitong bumati. Nang makita ni Kate si Vincent na papalapit, agad siyang nagtago sa likod ng isang Roman column. Ngunit nakita na siya ni Mitch. “Hey! Vincent! Over here! Come here!” sigaw nito habang kumakaway. Mula sa likod ng pader, nakita ni Kate si Vincent at ang ka-partner niya na papunta kina Mitch. Inakbayan ni Mitch ang braso ni Vincent at marahang inuga. “Vincent, I want to buy this watch. Okay?” “Of course.” sagot niya, nakatingin kay Mitch ng puno ng lambing. May liwanag sa mga mata niya, buhay, masigla—hinding-hindi niya nakikita kapag kasama siya sa bahay. “Thank you, Vincent! I’ll go swipe the card!” masayang sabi ni Mitch habang iwinagayway ang supplementary card. Napangiti rin ang ka-partner niya. “Mr. Vincent and Mrs. Vincent, you’re really such a loving couple. Nakaka-touch.” Mr. Vincent? Mrs. Vincent? Nagulat sina Vincent at Mitch.Ngunit… walang kahit isa sa kanila ang tumama sa sinabi ng business partner ni Vincent. CHAPTER SEVEN TAHIMIK na pinagmamasdan ni Kate sina Vincent at Mitch. Matapos ang ilang segundong ilangan, mabilis nilang tinanggap ang bagong papel nila at magkausap na sila nang masaya kasama ang mga business partners, nagtatawanan, parang walang iniisip. Bagay talaga sila… Tahimik na kinuhanan ni Kate ng litrato ang eksena. Pero nang tumalikod na siya at maglakad palayo, parang may karayom na muling bumaon sa puso niya. Isang matalim at paulit-ulit na sakit ang kumalat sa dibdib niya, hanggang sa pati dulo ng ilong niya ay parang naninikip sa sama ng loob.. “Kate!” Bago pa siya tuluyang makalabas ng mall, may tumawag sa kanya. Paglingon niya, may isang taong nakatayo sa pababang escalator, todo-kaway sa kanya. Hindi siya nagkakamali..Teacher niya iyon. Ang dating guro niya sa dance academy. “Ma’am Agatha!” Napasigaw siya sa tuwa. Mabilis bumaba ang guro at hinawakan ang dalawang kamay niya, halatang masaya rin. “Sabi ko na nga ba ikaw ‘yan! I just had a feeling. Kumusta ka na? Five years na ‘di ba? Ang tagal na nating hindii nagkikita.” Biglang bumigat ang dibdib ni Kate. Limang taon na ang lumipas… at pakiramdam niya, wala siyang narating. Ano bang mukha ang ihaharap ko sa kanya? “Busy ka ba? If you’re not, mag-afternoon snacks tayo,” aya ng guro, mahigpit pa ring hawak ang kamay niya. Hindi siya busy. Noong dati, baka tumanggi siya dahil sa hiya, sa takot, sa paglayo niya sa mundo ng sayaw. Pero simula noong buksan niya muli ang album ng mga lumang video niya sa pagsasayaw, parang may bitak na bumukas sa madilim niyang langit. Parang gusto na niyang papasukin muli ang liwanag. Tumango siya. “Sige po, Ma’am.” Hindi niya alam kung bakit, pero biglang nangilid ang luha sa mga mata niya. Magkasabay silang pumunta sa isang English-style afternoon café sa gitna ng ground floor. “Ma’am, kumusta na po ang mga kaklase ko?” tanong ni Kate. Matagal na siyang wala sa mundo nila, lahat ng group chat, matagal na niyang iniwan. Sinulyapan siya ng guro, parang may binabasa sa mukha niya. “Gusto mo ba talagang malaman?” Alam ng guro ang nangyari sa kanya, ang biglang pag-atras niya sa slot para sa graduate studies, ang aksidente, pati ang pagbisita nito sa kanya noon. Mariin siyang tumango. At nagkuwento ang guro. Limang taon, sapat para baguhin ang buhay ng isang tao. May mga kaklase siyang naging sikat ng ballerina sa ibang bansa. May iba namang nag-aral sa abroad at ang iba naman ay doctor, abogado... May ilan ding nanatili sa eskwelahan bilang mga guro, nagtuturo ng bagong henerasyon. Lahat sila ay umandar ang buhay. Siya lang ang naiwan. Pero hindi na mula ngayon. Mula ngayon, hahabol ako. Kahit hindi na ako makasayaw, hahanapin ko ang lugar ko sa mundo. “Ma’am… I think I can finally submit my answer sheet to you,” nanginginig ang boses niya, mainit ang mga mata sa luha. “Good,” ngumiti ang guro gaya ng dati. “I’ve always believed in you.” Lumapit si Kate at ibinulong ang plano niyang mag-aral sa abroad. Napahigpit ang hawak ng guro sa kamay niya. “That’s wonderful! I knew it! My student is no coward!” Bigla itong may naalala. “By the way, may European tour kami. Sama ka. Para ma-experience mo ang buhay doon.” “Pero Ma’am…Kaya pa ba ng paa ko? Hindi na siya pwedeng sumayaw. Kahit paglalakad, mabagal na siya. Theoretical pa ang kukunin niyang master’s. “No excuses!” mariing sabi ng guro. “Kung hindi ka naaksidente noon, kasama ka na sana sa La Prima Ballet. This time, sasama ka as staff, runner, stage crew, makeup assistant. Anything!” Diretso at walang awa pero hindi siya itinuring na kawawa. Napangiti si Kate. Gusto niya ang pakiramdam na iyon. Hindi dahil hindi na siya makasayaw ay wala na siyang silbi. Biglang nag-vibrate ang cellphone ng guro. “My husband,” paliwanag nito. “Okay lang bang sumama siya?” “Of course po,” sagot ni Kate, nakangiti. Pero sa loob-loob niya, may kaba. Limang taon siyang nagkulong sa sarili. Hindi na siya sanay sa mga bagong tao. Pero kailangan niyang magsimula. Ilang sandali lang at doon niya nakita. Papunta sa kanila sina Vincent, Mitch, at ang asawa ni Maam Agatha. Nang makarating sila sa mesa, nanatiling nakaupo si Kate. Tahimik niyang pinanood kung paano namutla at namula ang mukha nina Vincent at Mitch—sunod-sunod, parang eksena sa pelikula. “Please, have a seat,” sabi ng lalaki. “This is my wife, Agatha, a ballet dance teacher. And this is Mr. Vincent Fuentebella, my business partner. This is his wife.” Sa salitang “wife”, bahagyang nanginig ang kamay ni Vincent. Si Mitch naman, halatang hindi mapakali. Tahimik lang na ngumiti si Kate. “Ahmmm Kate, siya nga pala ang asawa ko. Si Nelson,” pakilala ng guro, sabay turo kay Kate. “And guys, ito naman ang student ko noon, siya ang may pinakamalaking tsansang manalo bilang ballerina noon. Pinakamagaling sumayaw na nakilala ko sa buong mundo.” Sa salitang iyon, tuluyang dumilim ang mga mata ni Vincent. Bumaba ang tingin niya tila gustong silipin ang mga binti ni Kate. Nakita niya ang sakit sa mga mata nito. Oo… masakit talaga. Kung hindi siya napilay noon, hindi siya pakakasalan ni Vincent. At ang babaeng nasa tabi niya ngayon, siya sana ang legal na asawa. Ngumiti si Kate. “Ma’am Agatha, Sir, Nelson actually, ako po ang—” “Ah!” Biglang napasigaw si Mitch. Natapon ang mainit na kape sa kamay nito at sa damit niya. “S-sorry! I’m so sorry! Ang clumsy ko,” pagmamadali niyang sabi, nag-aabot ng tissue. “Okay lang, okay lang,” sabi ng guro, walang kamalay-malay. Isang tasa ng kape ang pumigil sa katotohanan. Pero kung gusto talagang magsalita ni Kate… mapipigilan ba siya? Tumingin si Vincent sa kanya na parang humihingi ng tulong. Bahagyang umiling, pabulong ang labi. “Please… don’t say it. Relax, gusto niyang matawa. Hindi rin naman niya balak sabihin. Sinadya niya niya ang kalahating pangungusap dahil gusto lang niyang makita kung gaano mataranta ang mga ito.. Sa afternoon snacks na iyon..May mga taong parang nakaupo sa mga tinik. At may isang taong kalmado, tahimik na umiinom ng kape. Habang inaabot ni Kate ang tasa, napansin ng guro ang kamay niya. “Kate… married ka na pala? Sino ang husband mo?” Parang kidlat sa maliwanag na langit na nanlaki ang mata nina Vincent at Mitch. Tumingin si Kate sa kamay ni Vincent, walang suot na singsing. Ang wedding ring nila? Matagal na nitong tinanggal matapos ang kasal. Kung nasaan man iyon ngayon, baka natabunan na ng alikabok. “Five years na po,” sagot ni Kate ng tahimik. “Apelyido ng asawa ko ay Fuentebella.” “Talaga? Same surname?” mabilis na sabi ni Vincent. Halatang nataranta.. “Yes,” sagot niya, humigop ng kape “Businessman din siya. Hindi lang kasing laki ng negosyo ninyo,” sagot pa ni Kate na nakatingin kay Vincent. Kitang-kita niya kung paano bumuntong-hininga si Vincent sa likod ng tasa. “Ang galing ng coincidence,” sabi ni Nelson “Next time, sama-sama tayo. Dalhin mo rin ang husband mo, Kate.” Muling nag-iba ang kulay ng mukha ni Vincent. Limang taon silang kasal pero ang dami niyang ekspresyon ngayong hapon. Hindi na rin siya nagtagal. Nagpaalam siya, sinabing may meeting pa. Pero bago umalis, tinignan niya si Kate parang nagmamakaawa. Sumama ka na rin. Takot siyang baka may masabi pa siya. At si Kate? "He said he wasn't ready to talk about it but I have a feeling he is scared to tell me" she says. I place the empty plate on the table by my bed before I focus back on Rebecca. "A month ago I had the perfect family. Don't get me wrong we had our fights but we loved each other. My mom and dad always seemed so in love. Then one day I came home from school and found my mother k*ssing Xavier. A few days later I'm being told that my parents are getting a divorce. My mother and Connor effectively replaced my father. If that wasn't bad enough I was forced to leave my father alone because my mother and Xavier took my father to court for custody." "My father was heartbroken. First he lost his wife and son. Now they have taken me leaving him to face all of this by himself. When I talked to him last night I could tell he was drinking. My father never drinks. He is drowning his sorrows. How can my mother and Connor just cast him aside like he means nothing?" Warm tears flow down my cheeks. I don't think I have cried this much in my whole life. Rebecca moves cl*ser and pulls me into a h*g. "I'm so sorry that their decisions have hurt you and your father. Neither of you deserve this pain. I know now there are things that they haven't told you because I asked your brother why you didn't know what a Luna and Alpha are, but that doesn't excuse what's happened. I may be your brother's girlfriend but I hope to be your friend Olivia. Some day I hope you will consider me your sister," she says. I pull back and she giggles. "You look like one of those goldfish with the big eyes" she says. "I'm just shocked to hear you talk about marriage. How long have you two been dating?" "I know you don't want to but you really need to speak to your mother about this place and Xavier. You don't have to forgive her but you deserve answers and unfortunately I've been ordered to not spill any secrets" she says. "Ordered, what the hll is this place, a radical group?" She throws her head back and laughs. "I promise it's not a cu1to. Please just think about what I said. What do you plan to do today" she asks. "I'll probably just watch TV or read books on my phone. I'm in the middle of a biker romance on the Dreame app called The Biker's True Love. It is pretty steamy." "Sounds like my kind of book. Are you sure you don't want to get out of the room for a while" she asks. "Not today. I'm not ready to face anyone else right now." "That's alright. I'll be right by your side when you're ready. How about if I bring you lunch and we veg out and watch movies" she asks. "Are you sure you don't have plans with Connor?" "Connor is on my sh*t list right now. I would much rather spend time with you today." "Then I'll see you at lunchtime." She squeezes my hand before she slides off the bed and leaves my room. I lay back and pray I'm not making a mistake by letting Rebecca in but right now she is the only one I feel like I can trust. Connor POV I make my way through the pack house. A hundred thoughts swirling in my head. I know what's happened was out of our control, but seeing Oli so hurt is making it hard for me to breathe. It kills me to hear her say I'm no longer her brother. We have always been cl*se. I love her and it breaks my heart to be on the receiving end of her hate. I know her anger at me is because she thinks I don't care about dad, but I do. I love him just as much as she does. She also thinks I'm not angry at mom and Xavier, but she is wrong. I've just had more time to get my anger in check. Oli doesn't realize the secrets that mom and dad kept from us. That is part of the problem. Dad knew what mom was before they married. From what I was told, he embraced her despite the fact she kept such a huge secret from him. After she was pregnant with me he always knew there was a possibility that Oli and I would have the wolf gene. He was actually excited about the possibility of us having our own wolves from what he told me. He loved mom and her wolf, Jenna, too. He and mom were with me the first time I shifted. Mom and dad took me into the woods behind our home when the pain started. She told me what to expect a few months before my first shift, but nothing can prepare you for the pain. Don't get me wrong, it was worth every second of it, but to think you're human and then find out you're a wolf scr'ws with your head. The best part besides meeting Cosmo was the pride I saw in my dad's eyes when he saw my wolf for the first time. It is something I'll never forget. I wanted to tell Oli right away, but they insisted I wait. She was fourteen at the time. I wasn't told until I was seventeen, but I knew something was always off about how fast and strong I was. My parents didn't feel she was ready to hear about wolves having grown up among humans. Looking back, that was a huge mistake. We both should have been told when we became teenagers. We should have been given time to adjust to the fact we were different. Oli should have been there when I shifted. I wish I could go back and tell her the moment I found out we were wolves, but I can't. Dad and I had a long talk when he found out about Xavier and mom. It was funny to think about now but he was the voice of reason. I was so angry, just like Oli. He insisted that he loved me and that I didn't have to hate my mom on his behalf. It was difficult to listen to what he said until I met Rebecca. Even though I understood the pull of the bond, I hated seeing my father so broken. Despite everything that's happened, he still loves my mom desperately. My mother and I had a heated discussion about mates and the pain she was causing my father. You knew there was a chance you could meet your mate and, instead of waiting, you let yourself fall in love with dad." “It's not that simple, Connor. I wanted my love for your father to be enough, but it wasn't. Everything I felt for him was overshadowed by the instant love I felt for Xavier. I will always love Charles, but it pales in comparison to what I feel for Xavier. I hope you can forgive me," she says. Flashback Ends I'm still working on it. My chest aches when I think about how he must have felt the first time my mother told him about Xavier. When I told my dad about Rebecca, he wasn't angry at me for leaving. In fact, he insisted that finding her was a gift. He insisted I go to the pack to get to know her. He is so excited to meet her, despite his own pain. He always puts us first. I've seen him be loving with my mother, but normally he is all growly Alpha wolf. I hope that I never become that. He insists that I will be the next Alpha because of Rebecca, but I'm not really sure if that's what I want. I didn't even realize I knocked until the door opening breaks me out of my thoughts. My mother smiles when she sees it's me. She steps aside to let me in. Xavier is seated behind his large desk. I bear my n5ck as Cosmo, my wolf, has told me it is necessary to show respect to our Alpha wolf. "Connor, that isn't necessary. I consider you my son and someday you will be the alpha of the pack" he says. "With all due respect, Xavier, I have a father. It was the only fight I remember us having that scared me. After she reassured me of how much she loved me, I buried that fear. When Oli was born, I was wrapped around her little finger. I love both my kids the same, but she was my Oli girl. I never thought that all those years of happiness could be destroyed in a single meeting. I finish the bottle and it doesn't take long for the numbness to replace the memories and pain. I'm surrounded by darkness, but at least there is no more pain. Two Weeks Later Olivia POV The sound of the phone on my nightstand ringing wakes me from a deep sleep. When I look at the display, I see it's three in the morning. The number is one I've never seen before. I'm about to let it go to voicemail when something inside me has me answering. "Hello" I say. "Hello, is this Oli" a female voice asks. "Yes, who is this?" "My name is Miranda. I'm a nurse at Mercy Hospital. Are you related to Charles Crocker," she asks, and my blood runs cold in my veins. "Yes, I'm his daughter. What's going on?" She is the only person I trust in this place. "Oli, what's wrong," she asks, panic in her voice. I quickly explain everything to her. "Get dressed and meet me outside the front door" she says. My shoulders sag in relief before I throw on a pair of jeans and a sweatshirt. I open the door, praying no one is awake. The hall is quiet, and I move quickly down the hall toward the stairs. Once I make it through the foyer, I push open the front door slowly hoping it's not alarmed. Amazingly enough, nothing happens as I step out into the cold night air. "Oli" Rebecca says, scaring the sh*t out of me. I follow her down to an area of parked cars. "Your lucky my friend, is at the gate tonight, or we would have had to wake up the Alpha. I told him what's happening, and he agreed to help us," she says. I don't want my mother or Connor to know what's happening. They don't deserve to know after what they have done. "Will he get in trouble?" "No, I told him to tell Xavier I lied about having permission. My uncle won't punish me too harshly," she says. I stop in my tracks. "Did you just say that Xavier is your uncle?" "Come on Oli. We don't have time. I'll answer your questions on the drive to the hospital." A few minutes later we pull through the gate. My heart feels like it's going to beat out of my chest. As we drive away from my prison, the tears begin to fall again. I can't lose my dad. Rebecca tells me how her father and Xavier were brothers. When her parents died, Xavier took her in. I don't have time to focus on that as we pull up to the front of the hospital. "I can't tell you what this means to me, Rebecca. I'll call you as soon as I know anything," I say pulling her into a hvg. "Oh no way am I leaving you here by yourself. I know we haven't known each other long, Oli, but I consider you my sister. Let's go check on your dad" she says. We make our way inside and the nurse tells us where my dad's room is. We take the elevator and make our way to room 305. When I step inside, my knees nearly buckle at the sight of him. He is hooked up to machines and tubes surround him. My strong dad looks weak and frail. I say a silent prayer that he survives this. "Mr. Crocker, my name is Rebecca. I'm your son's mate and your daughter's best friend. I'm going to need you to wake up so I can meet you. Oli is here, and she needs you" she says. text: I Called The Police On The Man Next Door At Midnight. Then The Officer Walked Back Across The Yard And Took His Hat Off. The Larkins moved onto Fairlawn Street in February. I had the man figured out inside a week. I'd like to tell you it took longer than that. It didn't. He was big through the shoulders and he wore a heavy black vest most days, even in weather that didn't call for it. There was a scar on the left side of his face that ran from his ear down to his jaw, white and raised and old. He didn't wave. I've had 14 months to think about that week and I still can't make myself look good in it. He didn't wave, and I decided that meant something. He'd start his motorcycle in the dark and let it run in the driveway while he pulled his gloves on. Early, before the sky changed, when the whole street was still asleep. I'd lie there listening to that engine idle and I'd build a whole man out of it. I called the town about the noise ordinance in April. Renata told me to leave it alone. I told her somebody had to say something. Nothing came of the call and the mornings didn't change. By summer I'd stopped looking at that house at all. That was my version of being the bigger man. So that's who I was in August. A 67-year-old man who'd decided about a stranger and then spent 6 months collecting evidence for a verdict he'd already reached. Now the night. I don't sleep much anymore. I haven't in 10 years, and I've made a routine out of it. I go down, I sit in the kitchen with the light off, and I wait until it's late enough that going back up feels like a decision instead of a failure. That's what I was doing when I saw the light. It was a work light on a folding stand, and it was in the Larkins' backyard. I put my glasses on. Boyd Larkin was digging. He had a spade and he was working steady. The pile beside him was already up past his knee. And the hole looked long. It was long. It was in a shape I recognized without wanting to. Then I saw what was lying on the grass next to it. Something wrapped in a blanket. Green. Faded. In that light it was about the length of a person, and narrow. I was frightened, and underneath the fright there was something worse, and the worse thing was that I was glad. Glad I'd been right about him. I went to the phone in the hall so the light from the screen wouldn't show in the window. The dispatcher asked me to describe what I was seeing, and I heard my own voice say the words, and they sounded insane and also completely obvious. She asked if he had a weapon. I said, "He has a shovel." She asked me to stay inside. They came without sirens. That's the detail I didn't expect. 2 cruisers, no sirens, and no headlights. Renata came down in her robe because she'd heard me on the phone. I told her to stay back from the glass and she didn't. She stood next to me and put her hand flat on my back and we watched it happen without a word between us. An officer went up the Larkins' driveway on foot. Another went through the side gate. I could see slices of the yard through the fence slats. The work light. A shoulder. Boyd standing up straight with the spade laid down on the grass beside him and his hands out where they could be seen. Nobody shouted. I kept waiting for somebody to shout. It went on a long time. Long enough that Renata sat down at the table. Long enough that the coffee maker clicked over on its timer and neither of us moved to touch it. Then the officer came out of the gate and walked across the grass toward our side. His name was Vega. I found that out later. He was maybe 40 and he had a notebook in his hand and he stopped about halfway across, in the open, where I could see him. He stood there a second. Then he reached up and took his hat off and pressed it flat to his chest, and he stayed like that. A police officer standing in a dark yard with his hat in his hands, at a hole in the ground, at midnight. You already know I got it wrong. I didn't know it yet. Officer Vega came to the door. He asked if I was the caller. I said I was. He said, "Sir, there's no crime here." I said something stupid. I think I said, "There's a hole." He said, "Yes sir. There is." Then he told me. Boyd Larkin's wife had died 9 days earlier. Her name was Netta. The thing on the grass was her ashes, in a wooden box, wrapped in a quilt she'd made herself. Faded green with white stitching all over it, hand stitching, done small. It was a box the size of a bread tin, and I had stood at a window and built a grave around it. She'd asked to be put in the ground behind the house. The county allows it. You file for it. There's a setback you have to keep from the well, and there's a form that goes on the deed so that whoever buys that house someday knows what's in that yard. Boyd had the paperwork in a folder on his kitchen table. He'd had it for weeks. He'd had it since before she died, because she'd made him get it while she could still read it over. Vega said, "I went out there with my hand near my belt." He came back with his hat off. He'd read that form, and then he'd looked up at a man standing in a hole in the dark, alone, at midnight, doing a legal thing. I asked him why midnight. He said, "You'd have to ask him." I did ask him. It took me until the next afternoon to work up to it, and the answer was so plain it took the legs out from under me. Boyd said, "I didn't want an audience." He said, "Around here somebody's always in a window." There was another thing, and it landed on me that night. Renata was still at the kitchen table when Vega left. She hadn't moved. I said her name and she didn't look up, and then she said, "Cliff. I've been going over there." Tuesdays and Thursdays. Since March. She'd taken a pie over the week they moved in. She said, "Netta answered the door holding onto the frame with both hands, because she couldn't stay upright without it." So Renata started going. And then she started staying. For 5 months my wife had been walking next door to sit with a woman who was dying, and she had never once told me, and the reason she never told me was me. She said it straight out. She said, "You'd made up your mind about him and I didn't want to hear you say it in front of her house." She'd known for 9 days that Netta was gone, and she'd heard me on the phone saying the shape of that hole. She stood in the hallway and couldn't find a place to start, because the start was March. I asked her later why she hadn't taken the phone out of my hand. She said that stopping me would have meant starting, at midnight, standing next to that phone, with 5 months of it coming out at once. She said, "There was no short way to say it, and there never was going to be, because of the way you talked about him." 38 years married and my wife had a whole second life that ran on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons. She was protecting a woman who was dying from having to hear what her neighbor thought of her husband. I sat down in the chair across from her and I couldn't look at her. I called the police on the funeral. There was one mourner and one dead woman and one hole in the ground, and I called the police on it. He had to stop and go get the folder. That's the piece I can't put down. He was standing in a hole he'd dug for his wife, and a stranger's phone call made him climb out of it, walk into his own kitchen, and produce a document to prove he was allowed to bury her. Then when they'd gone he went back out and finished, because it was still only half done. The next day I walked over. I don't know what I was going to say. I got about as far as the end of his driveway and he came out the side door and stood on the step, and I ran out of road. I got out something about being sorry. He let me finish. Then he said, "She told me people would think what they think." He said, "She said if anybody ever called, I wasn't to hold it against them." And then he put his hand out. I took it. His hand was bigger than mine and there were 2 fingers on it that didn't straighten all the way, and he shook my hand like it was nothing. I found out later what the early mornings were. He'd taken a shift at a warehouse out on the county road so he could keep her at home instead of putting her in a facility. The noise I called the town about was a man going to work. None of the rest of this makes sense without my brother. Sam died in 2018. He was 59. Heart attack, in his own driveway, on a Saturday morning, with the car door open and the keys in his hand. His doctor had seen him 7 weeks before that and had told him his numbers were fine. The word he used was fine. Sam came out of that appointment and called me from the parking lot and said, "He cleared me." He was pleased about it, and I could hear he was pleased. Sam walked. He'd quit smoking in his 30s and never went back to it, not once, not at a wedding. He ate like a man who'd read the pamphlet and believed it, and he'd been doing all of it for 20 years before he died. He got a chart that said he was fine, and 7 weeks later he was on the concrete. So I stopped going. Here's the logic, and it isn't stupid logic. If a clean chart didn't save my brother, a chart doesn't save anybody. And if it doesn't save anybody, then getting one is just paying to be worried. I hadn't had blood drawn since 2018. Renata brought it up maybe twice a year and I had a laugh I did about it, a whole little routine, and eventually she stopped bringing it up. That was where I stood in August. 67 years old, no numbers, no intention of getting any, and a settled private theory that the whole business was theater. Netta Larkin had been a nurse for 30 years. She'd done cardiac work first and then hospice, which means the last stretch of her career was spent sitting in rooms with people who were dying and with the families who were watching it happen. Renata told me most of this after the burial, in pieces, over about a week, because she'd been carrying it alone. Boyd told me the rest across the fence. I asked Renata what they talked about, all those afternoons. She said, "Her patients, mostly." Netta had a thing she came back to. Renata said she brought it up more than once, near the end, when she was tired and less careful about what she said. She used to say that the charts of the men she'd nursed on the cardiac floor were so often fine. Not always. But so often. She'd been in the room, she'd read the file, and the file said the man was in acceptable shape, and the man was dying anyway. She said it bothered her for 30 years and nobody ever gave her a straight answer for it. And then Renata told me the other thing, and that one took the top of my head off. Netta's bed had been moved into the front room, because that's where the window was, and the window looked out at our porch. She watched me. She was a woman in a bed who couldn't do much else, and there was a street out there, and I was on it. And what she noticed, and mentioned to my wife more than once, was the stairs. I've got 4 steps up to my porch. That's all. 4. And she'd noticed that when I came up them with anything in my arms, I stopped at the top. Not for long. A couple of seconds. I'd get to the top step and I'd stand there with the bag or the mail or whatever it was and I'd wait, and then I'd go in. I did not know I did that. I can find it in my memory now that somebody's pointed at it, but I didn't know I did it, and Renata says she didn't either. Renata told me the words. She said Netta looked out the window one Thursday and said, "Get him seen." A woman I had never met, whose husband I'd reported to the town, was dying in a rented hospital bed 60 feet from my mailbox. She spent some of the attention she had left on me, and used it to tell my wife to get me to a doctor. I never spoke a word to her in my life. Renata got me an appointment for the middle of September and she didn't ask me. She told me at supper, and when I started up with my routine about it she put her fork down and said, "Cliff. She's in the ground and she was right about your steps." So I went. Dr. Soltis is on Beech Street and I hadn't been in that building since before Sam died. They took blood. I sat in the chair and watched the tube fill and thought about my brother in a parking lot, pleased. The call came 3 days later. My LDL was 181. Dr. Soltis read it off to me over the phone. He said, "One eighty-one," and then he waited. I said I understood. He talked about diet. He talked about walking. He said we'd draw it again in 3 months, and if the number was still sitting there we'd have a conversation about medication. I hung up and sat in my kitchen and felt exactly nothing, because I already knew a man with better numbers than that who was dead. I know how it sounds, a man who phoned the police on a funeral telling you what he learned from the widower. Boyd Larkin put in a garden that fall. Over her. Right over the plot, a raised bed, timbers and screws, and he filled it with the good soil from the far end of the yard. I'd be out at my fence and he'd be out at his, and we got into the habit of it, because neither of us wanted to be in the house. There were casseroles all that month. People from her old unit kept turning up with dishes, and Boyd couldn't eat a tenth of it, and he started handing them over the fence to us and I started taking them. He told me one afternoon that Netta had done a lot of reading about her own field once she was too sick to be in it. "She didn't have anything else to do but be right," he said. I asked him what took her, because I hadn't been able to ask before. He said, "Her heart was the last thing in her to quit." Then he asked me if I'd gotten my number. I told him 181, and I told him about Sam, and I told him my theory, the whole thing, the paying-to-be-worried theory. He didn't argue with it. "She'd have agreed with you about the chart," he said. Then he told me what she thought the chart was doing wrong, over about 3 weeks, at a fence, with a spade in his hand. The first part was hers, and Renata heard it too, so I've got it from both sides. He said, "The number on that panel is a count of how many LDL particles are moving through you." "Nobody at that lab looked at a single one of them to see what condition it was in," he said. Netta's version was blunter. She said she'd spent 30 years reading files that told her how many, and standing in rooms where the answer clearly wasn't how many. Second part. A particle like that can get damaged on the trip. The inside of it is fat. Around the outside of it there's a single protein that goes right round the whole thing, and it has a name, ApoB-100. There are reactive molecules moving through your blood at all times, and when they hit one of these particles they damage both halves. "They burn the fat inside and they chew on the wrapper," he said. Boyd said his wife used the word rancid about it, and then apologized for using it, because she said people hear rancid and picture something in the back of a cupboard. She said that's about right, though. Fat sitting somewhere warm with air getting at it, going off slowly, and the wrapper around it going off with it. He said, "A count doesn't know the difference." "It counts the rancid one and the clean one exactly the same and hands you one number for both." Third part, and this part is hers word for word, because Renata made her say it twice and wrote it down at the kitchen table. "The damage leaves fingerprints." "The burnt fat can be measured." "The wrapper protein can be looked at directly." "You can see where it's broken apart, and you can see where it's been chemically scarred, and where something's been tagged onto it that shouldn't be there." I said to Boyd, "I gave a year of my life to antioxidants once." He said, "It's a molecule with a name, doing a job somebody measured. Call it what you want." Here's where it turned into his part instead of hers. He drove a truck for 22 years and then he stacked pallets so his wife could die at home. He said the answer she'd landed on was tea, and he watched my face while he said it, and then he said, "Yeah. I know." I told him that year had been green tea. That's true. After Sam, for a year, I drank green tea every morning like it was a prescription, because it was the thing I could do that didn't require going into a building and being told a number. "Then you know the famous one," Boyd said. "EGCG." I said I'd seen it on the box. "Oolong," he said, "isn't green tea that got left out." "They oxidize that leaf on purpose," he said. That's the whole difference. Somebody takes the leaf and lets it oxidize under control, and stops it where they want it, and that process builds molecules the green leaf doesn't have. One of them is 2 EGCG units welded together into a single bigger molecule. He went in the house and came back with his wife's folder, and he found the page and held it out where I could read the word off it myself. Oolonghomobisflavan A. I laughed at him. I said, "That sounds made up." And then he told me the part I've since repeated to about 9 people. He said, "The controlled oxidation of the leaf is what builds the molecule that stands up to oxidation in the particle." "You oxidize the leaf on purpose so it can go do something about the oxidation you didn't ask for," he said. I asked him how anybody would even know that. He turned to the next page in that folder, because his wife had been the kind of woman who kept a folder. Some researchers took human LDL. Actual human particles, in a dish. They attacked them 3 different ways, on purpose, to be thorough about it. Peroxyl radicals first. Then peroxynitrite, which is one the body cooks up itself when there's inflammation. Then copper. Into all of it they put the oolong molecule. Then they went looking for the fingerprints. Fewer burnt fats inside. And the wrapper held. It came through with less of the breaking apart and less of the scarring, and the tagging was down too. Same answer down all 3 attack routes. That was 2017. Then Boyd said something I didn't expect, and he said it before I could. He said, "A dish isn't a person." He said it looking at the garden, not at me. He said his wife had been very firm about that. She'd watched 30 years of things that worked fine in a dish. And a dish has no liver in it, and no gut, and no 40 years of habits. I said, "So what good is it?" "It tells you the molecule can do the job," he said. "It doesn't tell you it does the job in a person." Then he told me about the people. Researchers put oolong catechins into 60 adults for 12 weeks. Blinded, placebo controlled, run properly. What they were measuring moved in the right direction. Nobody in that trial was handed a grocery teabag. They gave them a drink built to carry the catechins, at a level a mug of whatever's in your cupboard is never going to reach. So the trial isn't a promise about your kitchen. And then he closed the last gap himself. "None of it says a thing about the box in your own cupboard with the word oolong printed on the front," he said. Because the molecule is made by the processing. "Whole leaf, grown high, oxidized under control and stopped at the right place," he said. That's a manufacturing question. Dust in a paper sack with oolong on the front is a different product wearing the same word. He said, "Draw your own blood twice and stop taking my word for it." I got it wrong twice first. First I did the diet. 3 months of it, and I wasn't lazy about it. Red meat down to almost nothing, and I'm a man who'd cooked on a grill every Sunday since the kids left, so Renata will tell you what that cost the household. I walked a mile most days on the flat stretch by the school, and when it got cold I walked it anyway. I even gave up the 2 beers, which felt like the kind of sacrifice that ought to buy you something. The recheck came back and Dr. Soltis read it and it was sitting right up against 181 where I'd left it. He didn't even write it down while I was there. He said, "Some people just don't move much on diet," and he started in on medication again. I told him I wanted a little more time. He said, "Fine," and there was a lot loaded into it. He wrote it anyway, and I filled it that week, because I didn't have a reason not to. Second thing I did wrong. I went to the market and bought the cheapest box on the shelf with the word oolong on it. Drank it every morning through January. Nothing changed, and I told Boyd about it like a joke. He didn't laugh. He said, "What's in it?" Here are the numbers he gave me. The research level people are aiming at is somewhere around 150 milligrams a day. A supermarket bag of tea dust runs about 12 milligrams a cup. The ones with premium on the front, about 25. A decent whole leaf runs about 44. So the box I bought was delivering about 8 percent of what the research was built on, and I'd been drinking it like it was medicine and then using its failure as proof the whole idea was nonsense. Then Boyd told me how to do the thing he'd already told me to do. He said, "You can have your oxidized LDL drawn." Not the count. The condition of it. There's a walk-in out past the fairgrounds and they'll do it without a doctor's order. "You don't need anybody's permission for it," he said. I went the following Tuesday. The result came back 69 U/L. Under 60 is where they want you. I read it standing at the bottom of my own 4 steps with the mail still under my arm, and 2 things came at me at once. I'd looked at a man's scar and his vest and the hour he started his engine, and I'd built a whole person out of the outside of him, and I'd been wrong the entire time. And I'd looked at a number that counts how many and decided that was the whole of what could be known about me, and my brother had done exactly that and it buried him. I asked. Nobody ever drew that second number on Sam. It was available and nobody drew it, and his chart said fine. I ordered the good tea that night. Whole leaf, grown at altitude, 4 grams of it in the bag instead of the sweepings. It comes in at 187 milligrams of EGCG in a cup and 340 milligrams of polyphenols all in. That's nothing like 12. It clears the decent bag too. That's more leaf in the bag than a bag usually holds, grown higher, and left in the water longer. 1 cup, every morning, water hot but not boiling, 3 to 5 minutes. That's the whole protocol and it's boring. There's no ceremony to it. I make it while the dog eats. I gave it the winter and then I did both draws again on the same morning, the panel at Dr. Soltis's and the oxidized one out past the fairgrounds. LDL came back 155. Oxidized LDL came back 57. 57 is under 60. That number had been sitting under the cover the whole time, and I'd spent 67 years reading covers. I brought both papers to Dr. Soltis because I wanted to watch him. He looked at the panel first and said, "The pill's doing its job." He'd already decided where the result came from before he read it. Then I put the other sheet in front of him. He read it. He read it again. He asked me who ordered it. I said, "I did." And then he did the shrug. You know the one. Shoulders up and his hands out a little. He said, "Well. Keep doing whatever you're doing." That's the closest thing to a blessing I'm going to get and I've decided it's enough. He's a good doctor. He was trained on the count, and the count is what he goes by. I stayed on what he had me on. I didn't stop anything and I didn't ask to. The pill works on the count, and I've got no argument with the count getting smaller. It only ever had something to say about how many, and now I've got a number for the other half. But the number is the smaller part of this. Renata told me in April that I'd stopped stopping. I said, "Stopped stopping what?" She said, "The steps. You come up with the groceries and you come straight in." I made her tell me twice because I didn't believe her. Then I went out to the truck and got a bag and came up my own 4 steps and got to the top and kept walking, and I stood in my own hallway feeling like somebody had taken something off my back that I'd never known was on it. A dead woman found that from a bed she couldn't get out of. I couldn't tell you which of the things I changed took the pause off my steps. She never met me. She had every reason to think poorly of me, and she was right about my steps anyway. Boyd's garden came in. Tomatoes mostly, and garlic he'd put in over the winter, and it sits where it sits and neither of us calls it anything. This spring I took a spade to my own side of the fence and dug a bed against it, and I put in asparagus crowns. You can't cut asparagus the first year. Or the second. Boyd came over and looked at it and said, "That's optimistic." I said, "That's the idea." Renata still goes out on Tuesdays. She takes soup to a woman on Marbury Avenue now, and she comes home and tells me about it at supper, and she doesn't have to hide where she's been. So here's what I've got for you. I read a man by his cover and I read my own risk by its cover, and both times I was sure, and both times I was wrong. Open the actual thing. Go knock on the door. And then go get your oxidized LDL drawn, which you can do at a walk-in without anybody's order. The number you already have was only ever a roll call, and my brother's roll call was beautiful. The tea I drink every morning is here, and it's the same one I started on that winter. P.S. There's a 90 day money back guarantee on it. Which means trying it costs you nothing. If the number doesn't move for you, you get your money back and you'll still be holding the 2 results, which is more than I had a year ago. P.P.S. A woman who never spoke to me got me seen. That was Netta Larkin. She could barely get across a room by the end, and what she had left she spent on noticing that a man next door paused at the top of 4 steps. Then she said 3 words to my wife, and my wife ignored my whole routine about it and made the appointment without asking me. I'd been ungracious about being nagged for 8 years. I had a bit I did. I was good at it, and I used it to end the conversation every single time, and it worked, and it almost worked all the way. So if you're watching a man who won't go, and he's got a laugh he does about it, understand that the laugh is the defense. He built it so the conversation would end. Stop waiting for him to agree with you. Put a date on the calendar and tell him at supper. My wife is the reason I'm writing this instead of being written about. P.P.P.S. Keep taking whatever your doctor has you on. I did. I'm not asking you to stop a single thing. If this ever turns into an argument between you and your doctor, bring him the second sheet of paper and let the numbers do the talking. That's all I did. P.P.P.P.S. They're running buy 2 get 1 right now, which is what I do, because the whole thing only works if there's a bag in the cupboard on the morning you don't feel like it. Natural Relief in Weeks

text: Limang taon nang kasal, hindi kailanman ginalaw ni Vincent ang kanyang may kapansanang asawang si Kate, hanggang sa gabi bago bumalik ang kanyang unang pag-ibig... "Magdiborsyo na tayo," determinadong mungkahi ni Katei, habang papunta sa ibang bansa upang ituloy ang kanyang mga pangarap. Ngunit nang hindi sinasadyang makita ni Vincent ang resulta ng pregnancy test, tuluyan siyang nawalan ng kontrol… ** SA BANYO, maririnig ang tuluy-tuloy na lagaslas ng tubig. Si Vincent iyon, naliligo. Ala-tres na ng madaling-araw at kakauwi lang niya. Nakatayo si Kate sa tapat ng pinto ng banyo. May gusto sana siyang pag-usapan nila.. May kaba sa dibdib niya, and she wasn’t sure kung papayag ba ito sa sasabihin niya. Iniisip pa niya kung paano magsisimula, nang bigla siyang makarinig ng kakaibang tunog mula sa loob. She listened more carefully at saka niya lang naunawaan kung ano ang tunog na iyon. Ginagawa niya iyon mag-isa…Nagsasarili ang asawa niyang si Vincent sa loob ng banyo. Ang bawat hingal at pigil na ungol ay parang paulit-ulit na mabibigat na hampas sa kanyang dibdib. Ang sakit ay ganun na lamang. The pain came in waves, slowly spreading, drowning her, pulling her under until she could barely breathe. Samantalang ngayon ang mismong araw ng kanilang anniversary. Five years mula nang siya ay ikasal kay Vincent, at sa loob ng limang taon na iyon, ni minsan ay wala silang naging tunay na relasyon bilang mag-asawa. Ibig sabihin ba nito, mas pipiliin pa niyang gawin iyon mag-isa kaysa ang hawakan siya? Hindi niya maintindihan si Vincent. Habang lalong bumibilis ang paghinga nito, bigla narinig ni Kate ang pangalan na sinabi ng kanyang asawa na kanyang ikinagulat. “Mitch!!” Ang pangalang iyon ang ay parang kutsilyo na bumaon sa kanyang puso. Parang may sumabog sa loob ng kanyang dibdib. Parang may isang bagay na nadurog hanggang maging alikabok. Hindi niya kayang matanggap. Tinakpan niya ang kanyang bibig upang hindi makalabas ang iyak, tumalikod at tumakbo palayo sa pinto ng banyo ngunit sa unang hakbang pa lang ay nadapa siya, bumangga sa lababo, at tuluyang bumagsak sa sahig. “Kate?” Narinig pa rin ang boses ni Vincent mula sa loob ang kalabog, medyo humupa na ang kanyang ginagawa, pero halatang pilit niyang kinokontrol ang paghinga. “Ahhh… um… I’m fine…I just wanted to use the bathroom. Hindi ko alam na naliligo ka,” nauutal na sagot ni Kate. Isang kapos at halatang-halatang kasinungalingan, habang pilit siyang kumakapit sa lababo para makatayo. Ngunit habang mas nagmamadali siya, lalo siyang nagiging kawawa. Basang-basa ang sahig at ang lababo. Nakatayo na sana siya nang tuluyan nang biglang lumabas si Vincent. Naka-puting bathrobe ito, hindi maayos ang pagkakasuot sa pagmamadali, pero mahigpit ang pagkakatali ng sinturon sa baywang. “Nadapa ka ba? Let me help you.” Akmang hihilahin siya ng asawa ngunit itinulak niya palayo ang kamay ng asawa. Masakit pa rin ang katawan niya dahil sa pagkakadapa, namumuo ang luha sa kanyang mga mata pero mas masakit ang kanyang mga narinig. “Hindi na. Kaya ko,” tanggi niya sa alok na tulong ni Vincent. Muli siyang muntik madulas, saka siya paika-ikang tumakas pabalik sa kwarto. Tumakas. Eksaktong salita iyon. Sa limang taon na pagsasama nila ni Vincent, palagi siyang tumatakas. Tumatakas sa mundo sa labas. Tumatakas sa mga mapanghusgang tingin ng mga tao. At tumatakas sa awa at habag ni Vincent—Dahil siya…ay isang pilay. Paano nga ba babagay ang isang pilay sa isang lalaking perpekto, matagumpay, at hinahangaan ng lahat? Malinaw pa sa sikat ng araw na hindi siya nababagay sa kanyang asawa, pero noon ay maayos pa ang mga binti niya, binago lang naman ng isang aksidente ang lahat. Sumunod si Vincent sa kanya, malumanay ang tinig at puno ng pag-aalala. “Masakit ba? Let me see.” “Hindi… okay lang,” sagot niya. Mahigpit niyang hinigpitan ang kumot, itinago sa ilalim nito ang sarili kasama ang kanyang kahihiyan. “Talaga bang okay ka lang?” Totoo ang pag-aalala nito. “Oo,” sagot niya. Nakaharap siya palayo, mariing tumango. “Matutulog ka na? Hindi ba’t gusto mong gumamit ng banyo?” “Hindi na… let’s just sleep,” mahina niyang sabi. “Sige. Ah—by the way, anniversary natin ngayon. I bought you a gift. Buksan mo bukas, see if you like it.” “Sige,” walang gana niyang sagot. Nasa tabi ng kama ang regalo. Kahit hindi niya pa buksan, alam na niya kung ano ang laman. Pare-pareho ang laki ng kahon taon-taon. Pare-pareho rin ang laman—isang relo. Sa drawer niya, kasama ng mga regalo kapag birthday niya, may siyam na magkakaparehong relo na. Ito ang ikasampu. Hindi na nagbago ang ibinibigay nito. Paulit-ulit nalang. Doon na natapos ang usapan nila. Pinatay niya ang ilaw at humiga. Kumalat sa hangin ang amoy ng basang sabon mula sa pagligo ni Vincent, ngunit halos hindi niya maramdaman ang paglubog ng kama dahil sa dalawang metrong lapad nito, nakahiga siya sa isang gilid, si Vincent naman sa pinakadulo ng kabilang gilid. May pagitan pa, sapat para sa tatlong tao. Ganun sila kung matulog noon pa man…Hindi niya na binanggit ang narinig niya sa banyo at lalong hindi niya binanggit ang tungkol sa tinatawag nitong pangalan, para bang walang anumang nangyari. Matigas siyang nakahiga, nanlalabo ang paningin sa hapdi ng mga mata. Pigil na pigil niya ang pag-iyak… Mitch. Ang buong pangalan niya—Michelle Calderon. Kaklase niya sa kolehiyo. Unang pag-ibig at babaeng iniingatan ni Vincent sa kanyang puso. Pagkatapos ng kolehiyo, nagpunta si Mitch sa ibang bansa, kaya nagkahiwalay ang mga ito. Dahil sa nangyari ay labis na nalugmok si Vincent noon. Hindi niya natanggap na umalis ang babaeng mahal na mahal niya. Every day, he drank. Magkaklase sila ni Vincent noong high school. Aminado siyang noon pa man, lihim na niya itong nagustuhan. Ito ang campus crush, top student, cold aura. Si Kate naman ay isang art student, maganda rin, pero sa high school ang sukatan ay grades. Hindi kapansin-pansin ang mga artist students. Hindi rin napapansin si Kate ng lalaki. Kaya nanatili iyong isang lihim na pag-ibig. Ni minsan, hindi niya inisip na makakalapit siya rito at magiging mag-asawa sila.. Hanggang sa isang araw pagkauwi niya sa dance academy ay nadatnan niya itong miserable sa gitna ng daan…Gabi na. Lasing na lasing ito, pasuray-suray maglakad, tumatawid ng kalsada nang hindi tumitingin sa ilaw. Nang may napansin siyang paparating na sasakyan at mabilis na nagmamaneho ang driver, hindi na ito nakapagpreno dahil si Vincent ay tila walang pakialam. At dahil sinusundan niya ito at nag-aalala, itinulak niya ito palayo upang makaiwas sa sasakyan at siya ang nasagasaan na dapat ay ito. Isa siyang dancer. Gusto niya sanang mag-aral pa ng sayaw, ang maging isang sikat ng dancer balang araw ngunit dahil sa aksidente, napilay ang kanyang binti. She could never dance again. Sinulyapan siya ng guro, parang may binabasa sa mukha niya. “Gusto mo ba talagang malaman?” Alam ng guro ang nangyari sa kanya, ang biglang pag-atras niya sa slot para sa graduate studies, ang aksidente, pati ang pagbisita nito sa kanya noon. Mariin siyang tumango. At nagkuwento ang guro. Limang taon, sapat para baguhin ang buhay ng isang tao. May mga kaklase siyang naging sikat ng ballerina sa ibang bansa. May iba namang nag-aral sa abroad at ang iba naman ay doctor, abogado... May ilan ding nanatili sa eskwelahan bilang mga guro, nagtuturo ng bagong henerasyon. Lahat sila ay umandar ang buhay. Siya lang ang naiwan. Pero hindi na mula ngayon. Mula ngayon, hahabol ako. Kahit hindi na ako makasayaw, hahanapin ko ang lugar ko sa mundo. “Ma’am… I think I can finally submit my answer sheet to you,” nanginginig ang boses niya, mainit ang mga mata sa luha. “Good,” ngumiti ang guro gaya ng dati. “I’ve always believed in you.” Lumapit si Kate at ibinulong ang plano niyang mag-aral sa abroad. Napahigpit ang hawak ng guro sa kamay niya. “That’s wonderful! I knew it! My student is no coward!” Bigla itong may naalala. “By the way, may European tour kami. Sama ka. Para ma-experience mo ang buhay doon.” “Pero Ma’am…Kaya pa ba ng paa ko? Hindi na siya pwedeng sumayaw. Kahit paglalakad, mabagal na siya. Theoretical pa ang kukunin niyang master’s. “No excuses!” mariing sabi ng guro. “Kung hindi ka naaksidente noon, kasama ka na sana sa La Prima Ballet. This time, sasama ka as staff, runner, stage crew, makeup assistant. Anything!” Diretso at walang awa pero hindi siya itinuring na kawawa. Napangiti si Kate. Gusto niya ang pakiramdam na iyon. Hindi dahil hindi na siya makasayaw ay wala na siyang silbi. Biglang nag-vibrate ang cellphone ng guro. “My husband,” paliwanag nito. “Okay lang bang sumama siya?” “Of course po,” sagot ni Kate, nakangiti. Pero sa loob-loob niya, may kaba. Limang taon siyang nagkulong sa sarili. Hindi na siya sanay sa mga bagong tao. Pero kailangan niyang magsimula. Ilang sandali lang at doon niya nakita. Papunta sa kanila sina Vincent, Mitch, at ang asawa ni Maam Agatha. Nang makarating sila sa mesa, nanatiling nakaupo si Kate. Tahimik niyang pinanood kung paano namutla at namula ang mukha nina Vincent at Mitch—sunod-sunod, parang eksena sa pelikula. “Please, have a seat,” sabi ng lalaki. “This is my wife, Agatha, a ballet dance teacher. And this is Mr. Vincent Fuentebella, my business partner. This is his wife.” Sa salitang “wife”, bahagyang nanginig ang kamay ni Vincent. Si Mitch naman, halatang hindi mapakali. Tahimik lang na ngumiti si Kate. “Ahmmm Kate, siya nga pala ang asawa ko. Si Nelson,” pakilala ng guro, sabay turo kay Kate. “And guys, ito naman ang student ko noon, siya ang may pinakamalaking tsansang manalo bilang ballerina noon. Pinakamagaling sumayaw na nakilala ko sa buong mundo.” Sa salitang iyon, tuluyang dumilim ang mga mata ni Vincent. Bumaba ang tingin niya tila gustong silipin ang mga binti ni Kate. Nakita niya ang sakit sa mga mata nito. Oo… masakit talaga. Kung hindi siya napilay noon, hindi siya pakakasalan ni Vincent. At ang babaeng nasa tabi niya ngayon, siya sana ang legal na asawa. Ngumiti si Kate. “Ma’am Agatha, Sir, Nelson actually, ako po ang—” “Ah!” Biglang napasigaw si Mitch. Natapon ang mainit na kape sa kamay nito at sa damit niya. “S-sorry! I’m so sorry! Ang clumsy ko,” pagmamadali niyang sabi, nag-aabot ng tissue. “Okay lang, okay lang,” sabi ng guro, walang kamalay-malay. Isang tasa ng kape ang pumigil sa katotohanan. Pero kung gusto talagang magsalita ni Kate… mapipigilan ba siya? Tumingin si Vincent sa kanya na parang humihingi ng tulong. Bahagyang umiling, pabulong ang labi. “Please… don’t say it. Relax, gusto niyang matawa. Hindi rin naman niya balak sabihin. Sinadya niya niya ang kalahating pangungusap dahil gusto lang niyang makita kung gaano mataranta ang mga ito.. Sa afternoon snacks na iyon..May mga taong parang nakaupo sa mga tinik. At may isang taong kalmado, tahimik na umiinom ng kape. Habang inaabot ni Kate ang tasa, napansin ng guro ang kamay niya. “Kate… married ka na pala? Sino ang husband mo?” Parang kidlat sa maliwanag na langit na nanlaki ang mata nina Vincent at Mitch. Tumingin si Kate sa kamay ni Vincent, walang suot na singsing. Ang wedding ring nila? Matagal na nitong tinanggal matapos ang kasal. Kung nasaan man iyon ngayon, baka natabunan na ng alikabok. “Five years na po,” sagot ni Kate ng tahimik. “Apelyido ng asawa ko ay Fuentebella.” “Talaga? Same surname?” mabilis na sabi ni Vincent. Halatang nataranta.. “Yes,” sagot niya, humigop ng kape “Businessman din siya. Hindi lang kasing laki ng negosyo ninyo,” sagot pa ni Kate na nakatingin kay Vincent. Kitang-kita niya kung paano bumuntong-hininga si Vincent sa likod ng tasa. “Ang galing ng coincidence,” sabi ni Nelson “Next time, sama-sama tayo. Dalhin mo rin ang husband mo, Kate.” Muling nag-iba ang kulay ng mukha ni Vincent. Limang taon silang kasal pero ang dami niyang ekspresyon ngayong hapon. Hindi na rin siya nagtagal. Nagpaalam siya, sinabing may meeting pa. Pero bago umalis, tinignan niya si Kate parang nagmamakaawa. Sumama ka na rin. Takot siyang baka may masabi pa siya. At si Kate?
